title: PostgreSQL Index Types: B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, Partial, and Expression Indexes
description: PostgreSQL Index Types: B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, Partial, and Expression Indexes. Interview-first coverage of mechanisms, prediction, diagnosis, and trade-offs.
learningObjectives: Match PostgreSQL index families to operators and data shape.
Explain GIN, GiST, and BRIN trade-offs.
Use partial and expression indexes when predicates match.

mentalModel.text: Different indexes are like different lookup tools. A B-tree is a good everyday choice for exact values, ranges, and sorting. GIN is useful when searching inside arrays or JSON documents. BRIN summarizes large runs of nearby table pages. Pick the tool that supports the question your query is asking.

blocks.text: B-tree is the general-purpose starting point because it supports equality, range conditions, and ordered results. Hash is narrower: it supports equality lookups.

B-tree is the general-purpose choice for equality checks, ranges, and sorted results. Hash indexes support equality checks but not range searches or ordered output. Start with B-tree unless the query needs a different kind of search.

blocks.title: Match the index to the search
rows: Exact matches, ranges, and sorted results.
The everyday default for many scalar columns.

Can be larger and more expensive to update.
Spatial, range, and other searches supported by its operator class.
Its behavior depends on the operators and data type.

Small summary index; matching pages may need row rechecks.

blocks.problem: A query asks for all events between two timestamps and orders them by timestamp.
reasoning: A B-tree on timestamp can navigate to the range and return keys in order.
A hash index can help equality checks but cannot provide a timestamp range or sorted output.
Choose the index type that supports the operators and ordering the query needs.
blocks.outcome: Start with B-tree for common scalar searches unless the workload gives a clear reason to choose another type.

blocks.text: GIN is an inverted index: it maps each component to the rows that contain that component. This suits searches inside composite values such as arrays and JSONB.

A GIN index helps find rows that contain a particular component, such as a value inside an array or a key/value pattern inside JSONB. It stores a lookup from each component to the rows that contain it, so it is useful for supported containment and text-search queries.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE INDEX products_attrs_gin ON products USING GIN (attributes jsonb_path_ops);

blocks.problem: An events table has JSONB tags and the query asks for events whose tags contain 'security'.
reasoning: A GIN index can index components inside the JSONB value.
The query must use an operator supported by the chosen GIN operator class.
GIN can use significant storage and add write work, so validate the plan and write workload.
blocks.outcome: GIN can speed up containment-style searches that a simple B-tree on the whole JSON document may not support well.

reasoning: A regular B-tree on the entire JSONB value is not the general tool for this containment search.
A GIN index with an operator class that supports the `@>` containment operator can index the document's components.
The query must use an operator supported by that operator class. GIN's extra entries also increase index size and write cost.
blocks.outcome: Choose an index by the operator the query uses and the data shape—not simply because a column is JSONB.
blocks.problem: A product's `attributes` JSONB column stores color, size, and material. The endpoint asks for products whose attributes contain `{"color":"blue"}`.

blocks.text: GiST supports several operator families, including spatial and range searches. BRIN stores summaries for groups of nearby table pages and works best when physical order correlates with the searched value.

GiST supports different kinds of searches, including some geometric and range operations. BRIN stores a small summary for groups of nearby table pages. BRIN is compact and useful when nearby pages contain similar values, such as timestamps inserted in order, but PostgreSQL may need to recheck matching rows.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE INDEX events_created_brin ON events USING BRIN (created_at);

blocks.problem: A huge append-only events table is mostly inserted in timestamp order and reports filter by a broad time range.
reasoning: BRIN can summarize minimum and maximum timestamps for groups of pages.
PostgreSQL can skip page ranges whose summaries cannot match, but it may need to recheck rows in selected pages.
If timestamps are scattered randomly through the table, the summaries become less useful.
blocks.outcome: BRIN is compact when nearby pages contain similar values; GiST fits searches supported by its operator class.

blocks.text: A partial index contains only rows that satisfy a condition, so it can be smaller when queries repeatedly target a stable subset.

A partial index includes only rows that meet a condition, such as jobs whose status is 'pending'. It can be smaller than an index on every job. PostgreSQL can use it only when it can prove that the query asks for rows covered by that condition.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE INDEX jobs_pending_created_idx ON jobs (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

blocks.prompt: Does the existence of an index guarantee PostgreSQL will use it?
blocks.explanation: The planner compares estimated costs, and another access path may be cheaper.

blocks.problem: A jobs table has ten million completed jobs but only a few thousand pending jobs, and workers repeatedly claim pending jobs.
reasoning: Create an index on scheduling columns with a predicate such as WHERE status = 'pending'.
Queries must imply that predicate for PostgreSQL to use the partial index.
A parameterized condition can prevent the planner from proving the predicate in some plans, so test the actual prepared query.
blocks.outcome: Partial indexes can keep a hot subset small, but the query predicate must match the index condition.

reasoning: Create a partial index containing only pending jobs, ordered by creation time.
The queue query must include a condition PostgreSQL can recognize as implying `status = 'pending'`.
If the query uses a generic prepared parameter for status, PostgreSQL may not be able to prove that the predicate always matches the partial index; test the actual prepared plan.
blocks.outcome: Partial indexes save space by indexing only a useful subset, but their predicate must line up with the query PostgreSQL plans.
blocks.problem: A job queue repeatedly asks for the oldest pending jobs, while most historical jobs are completed.

blocks.text: An expression index stores the result of an expression, so a query can search using the same expression instead of calculating it for every row.

An expression index stores the result of a calculation, such as lower(email), instead of only the original column. It can help when queries use that same expression, but the query must match the indexed expression closely and PostgreSQL requires index functions to be immutable.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_lower_email_uq ON users (lower(email));

blocks.problem: Email lookups should be case-insensitive and queries use lower(email) = lower($1).
reasoning: Create an index on lower(email), not only on the raw email column.
Write the predicate using the indexed expression so PostgreSQL can match it to the index.
Define a consistent normalization and uniqueness policy if differently cased emails should count as the same address.
blocks.outcome: Expression indexes help when the application consistently queries through that expression; they also add write cost.

blocks.text: 1. Problem and motivation — A service filters scalar IDs, searches inside JSONB tags, and scans date ranges in a large append-oriented table. One index family will not serve every operator equally well.

2. Definition and design choice — Index families support different operators and data layouts: B-tree handles common equality, range, and ordering work; GIN supports membership in composite values; GiST supports operator families such as spatial and range searches; BRIN summarizes nearby heap-page ranges.

steps.title: Partial indexes
steps.description: A partial index contains only rows that satisfy a condition, so it can be smaller when queries repeatedly target a stable subset.

blocks.problem: An API queries `customer_id = 42`, searches JSONB with `metadata @> '{"urgent": true}'`, and analytics filters a date range on a table inserted mostly in timestamp order.
reasoning: A B-tree on customer_id suits scalar equality; a GIN index may support JSONB containment; a BRIN index can be compact when timestamps correlate with physical page order.
A partial index can omit rows outside a stable predicate, and an expression index can index a frequently used expression. Query operators and predicates must match index semantics.
Specialized indexes differ in size, build time, and update cost. Even a suitable index can lose to a sequential scan when most rows match.
blocks.outcome: Choose from actual operators, data distribution, and physical layout; verify operator-class support and compare read benefits with index maintenance.

blocks.title: 5. Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: Index type follows operators and data shape, not column labels.

blocks.prompt: 6. Interview probe — Which is the default starting point for scalar equality, range, and ordered scans?
blocks.answer: B-tree supports equality, range, and compatible ordering.
blocks.explanation: A strong answer connects the problem to the mechanism, states assumptions and trade-offs, and explains how to verify the decision in practice.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Trade-off 1
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Index type follows operators and data shape, not column labels.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Trade-off 2
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: GIN can be costly to update; BRIN depends on physical correlation; partial/expression indexes require predicate/expression matching.

revisionSheet.text: B-tree supports common equality, range, and ordering patterns.
GIN is an inverted index for supported component-search operators.
GiST is operator-class-specific; BRIN summarizes physical block ranges.
Partial indexes contain only rows matching their predicate.
Expression indexes need compatible expressions and immutable functions.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A PostgreSQL table has JSONB attributes and timestamps. Product needs JSONB containment and time-range reports. Recommend indexes.
strongAnswerPoints: Evaluate GIN for JSONB containment with a suitable opclass.
Evaluate B-tree for ordered time ranges; BRIN if huge and physically correlated.
Measure index size, write rate, rechecks, and plans.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would evaluate GIN for JSONB containment and B-tree for time-range/order queries. For a huge append-oriented table with strong time-to-heap-order correlation, BRIN may be smaller but lossy. Confirm operators/opclasses and benchmark using EXPLAIN ANALYZE and buffers.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A partial index on status='pending' is not used by a prepared query with a status parameter. What do you check?
strongAnswerPoints: Check if the planner can prove the query implies the index predicate.
Inspect generic/custom plan behavior where relevant.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: The planner must prove the query predicate implies the partial-index predicate. A generic parameterized plan may not know the value is always pending. Inspect the actual plan and prepared-plan behavior before changing the design.
